title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 19 Oct 2026]
Title:EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI-BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command-line interface with two runtime-budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six-dimensional framework (M1-M6) whose buckets are populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark-level averages. We describe the suite, the sub-metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost-efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT-4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt-5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at this https URL.

report.summary: EGI-BENCH unifies eight enterprise agent benchmarks into one CLI and a six-dimensional EGI Score, revealing no single LLM dominates enterprise capabilities.
report.background: Enterprises are moving LLMs from chat demos into agentic workflows that touch CRM records, documents, personal data, planning, tool calls, and long-horizon software work. But the evaluations used to justify those deployments are scattered across separate repositories, each with its own runner, dependencies, and scoring conventions. That fragmentation makes cross-benchmark comparison expensive and can hide what an aggregate score actually measures. A model that excels at retrieval may fail at safety abstention or multi-turn planning, yet a single leaderboard number flattens those distinctions. EGI-BENCH responds by consolidating eight enterprise-facing agent benchmarks behind one command-line interface with runtime-budgeted quick and deep modes. It also proposes an Enterprise General Intelligence Score that routes fine-grained sub-metrics into six capability dimensions, aiming to give buyers, developers, and researchers a more comparable and interpretable view of enterprise agent readiness.
key_points: The suite bundles CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE and LOCOBENCH behind a single CLI. Two runtime-budgeted modes—quick and deep—let teams trade off evaluation cost against depth, reducing the integration burden of running separate benchmark runners and scoring scripts.

Instead of averaging benchmark-level scores, the EGI Score is a six-dimensional framework (M1–M6) populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark. This is meant to show which capabilities drive an aggregate result—such as planning, retrieval grounding, tool actioning, safety/abstention, or engineering quality—rather than collapsing everything into one opaque number.

In quick-mode tests of 14 frontier and cost-efficient GPT, Claude and Gemini models, top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 for GPT-4o mini to 65.6 for gpt-5.5. The spread suggests enterprise agent performance still varies widely even among current commercial models.

No model dominates every axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. The result argues for capability-specific model selection and routing rather than a single overall winner.

The paper reports only quick-mode results and describes suite design, sub-metric routing and budgets; deep-mode results and production validity remain to be tested. Code is released, so reproducibility and community scrutiny are possible.
report.impact: For the AI industry, EGI-BENCH pushes enterprise agent evaluation toward standardized, multi-axis reporting. It could influence procurement by making capability trade-offs visible—safety and tool use versus planning and retrieval—instead of rewarding a single leaderboard score. For developers, a unified CLI and sub-metric routing reduce harness engineering and make cross-model comparisons more reproducible; expect teams to adopt similar routing for internal evals. For regular users, the practical payoff is better-matched agents: a model chosen for safe abstention in customer data tasks may differ from one chosen for long-context coding. The caveat is that benchmarks are proxies; quick-mode results and synthetic enterprise tasks may not predict production reliability, so organizations should validate on their own workflows.
report.tools: Start with the EGI-BENCH code release and paper. Track constituent suites for targeted testing: CRMARENA for CRM operations, HERB for heterogeneous-document retrieval, PERSONABENCH/USERBENCH for personal data and user modeling, MCP-UNIVERSE/MCPEVAL for tool use and function calling, BENCHFORCE for long-horizon research, and LOCOBENCH for long-context software engineering. Pair them with internal task traces and human review before procurement.
